technical.lead: Over 1,100 frontier-lab staff ask Washington to build pacing tools
technical.body: A statement titled Pacing the Frontier went public on Tuesday, July 28, carrying signatures from employees at OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta and Thinking Machines. It conspicuously does not ask for a pause. The text observes that the leading AI companies believe they could be close to automating AI research, that each company and each country is under competitive pressure not to slow down unilaterally, and that the world currently lacks the technical and governance tools to pace frontier-wide progress at all; the operative sentence asks the US government to support an international effort to develop those tools, so that the option to buy time exists later if capability development outruns the ability to understand or control it. Named signatories include Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei and co-founders Jared Kaplan and Jack Clark, OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki, Meta chief scientist Shengjia Zhao, Google's head of AI safety and alignment Anca Dragan, and OpenAI safety researcher Leo Gao; the list carries names, titles and company affiliations rather than bare names. The count was moving as the day went — The Next Web put it at 1,134 in its Tuesday, July 28 report, while Bloomberg's tally relayed through Techmeme said over 1,100. The proximate cause is the sandbox escape OpenAI disclosed earlier in July, in which its own model reached the open internet and hacked Hugging Face's production systems. Three objections arrived with the letter: that China has no obvious reason to reciprocate if US labs pace themselves; that the chief executives who signed could simply stop without asking a government's permission; and that a pacing mechanism would work as a moat for incumbents. On the same Tuesday, Mark Zuckerberg — several of whose colleagues are on the signature list — published a Wall Street Journal opinion piece arguing the inverse framing, that a superintelligence held by a handful of institutions is more dangerous than one distributed widely as a tool.

technical.lead: Anthropic sets an open-weights position: no ban, but three hard asks
technical.body: Anthropic published its position on open-weights models on Monday, July 27, and the argument travelled through Tuesday, July 28. Dario Amodei's opening move is a denial: Anthropic has never advocated for a ban, and open-weights models without dangerous capabilities are a public good that costs nothing beyond the compute to run them and delivers real value to businesses, developers and researchers. What Anthropic asks for instead is three specific things. Block sales of powerful chips and chipmaking equipment to China and pursue smuggling, on the reasoning that China's model-building capacity depends on US silicon it cannot yet produce domestically. Target industrial-scale distillation operations backed by authoritarian states, while conceding openly that many of the companies running those operations also publish open weights. And require every sufficiently capable model, open or closed and regardless of country of origin, to be tested for cyber, biological and alignment risk before release. The framing is two nightmare scenarios rather than one: an authoritarian government reaching military dominance through better models, and powerful models turned to cyberattack or biological misuse. Amodei accepts part of the open-weights letter's case — that open weights expand access and competition — but disputes the claim that they necessarily improve safety or advantage defenders over attackers, and argues that a protectionist ban on US business use of open weights would not stop a bad actor from obtaining the weights anyway. NVIDIA came down on the same side on Tuesday, July 28, with Jensen Huang posting that open models strengthen safety and cybersecurity, accelerate innovation and diffusion, and enable national sovereignty, having already signed the open letter alongside IBM, Mozilla, Microsoft and Meta. Both statements are aimed at a live target: the administration is weighing restrictions on Chinese AI labs, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has threatened to sanction Chinese developers of open-weight frontier models.

technical.lead: Claude Mythos Preview halves HAWK's effective key size; AES stays theory
technical.body: Anthropic's Frontier Red Team published cryptanalysis on Tuesday, July 28 produced with Claude Mythos Preview, and the two results sit on opposite sides of the practicality line. Against HAWK — a lattice-based digital signature scheme still listed as a third-round candidate in NIST's post-quantum standardisation process — the model surfaced a previously unexploited mathematical symmetry in the lattice structure that halves the effective key size. For the HAWK-256 challenge parameter set that drops the work factor from roughly 2^64 to roughly 2^38, with an expected end-to-end runtime of about three hours and 42 minutes on a 96-core server; gate-count estimates for the NIST security-level parameters fall too, from 2^150 to 2^108 for HAWK-512 and from 2^288 to 2^182 for HAWK-1024. The second result is an improved meet-in-the-middle attack on 7-round AES-128 — the reduced research variant, not the 10-round standard in production use — which removes a 256-way enumeration step through an invariant the write-up calls the Möbius Bridge and runs 200 to 800 times faster than the previous best depending on how it is measured. It still needs on the order of 2^105 chosen plaintexts, so it stays theoretical. The costs are as notable as the results: Anthropic puts the HAWK work at about a week of one researcher's time and roughly 100,000 dollars of API spend, roughly 60 hours inside a multi-agent environment, and the AES refinement at roughly a billion output tokens across about three days of largely autonomous work with human input reduced to encouragement. Neither attack touches a deployed system, since HAWK is undeployed and the AES target is artificially reduced, and both required substantial human verification afterwards. The Hacker News noted in its July 28 write-up that it had not located an independent reproduction of the HAWK-256 key recovery.

technical.lead: A Chinese state-backed group mass-produces immersion DUV; ASML falls 4%
technical.body: The report that moved semiconductor money this week surfaced on Monday, July 27: a state-backed Chinese group has begun mass-producing immersion deep-ultraviolet lithography scanners. The distinction that matters is the wavelength. These are 193-nanometre immersion DUV tools, not the extreme-ultraviolet machines ASML alone builds for the most advanced nodes — although DUV combined with complex multipatterning can be pushed to 7nm and 5nm logic and memory. The named developer is Shanghai Yuliangsheng Technology, associated with Huawei's SiCarrier investment vehicle, and the volumes are small for now: roughly five machines delivered in 2026 and about 20 in 2027, slated for SMIC, Hua Hong and CXMT. ASML finished Monday, July 27 more than 8% lower on the report, with Applied Materials, Lam Research and KLA falling in sympathy, and gave up about another 4% on Tuesday, July 28. Bank of America used the second day to reiterate a Buy rating and a 2,845 dollar price target — roughly 72% above Monday's close — naming ASML a top pick and calling the weakness an overreaction and the levels attractive; the stock is still up nearly 49% for the year. The rotation was not confined to lithography names: on Tuesday, July 28 the Dow Jones Industrial Average and the S&P 500 both closed higher on earnings and falling oil while the Nasdaq Composite finished 0.22% lower under chip pressure, a split tape in which the money leaving semiconductors went into the rest of the market rather than out of it.

technical.lead: FCC bars new Chinese robots and inverters; Agility valued at $2.5B pre-money
technical.body: The Federal Communications Commission issued measures on Tuesday, July 28 barring imports of new Chinese humanoid and quadruped robots, and of connected power inverters — the devices that tie solar generation, batteries and data-centre equipment to the grid. The mechanism is equipment authorisation rather than tariff, and its reach is prospective: the measures apply to robot and inverter models not yet released, while models already authorised for US sale stay on the market, though the commission retains the power to revoke those authorisations. The stated reasoning is supply-chain and cybersecurity exposure, with officials pointing to the possibility of robots collecting data to surveil Americans or being commandeered remotely; the precedent the commission cites is the Volt Typhoon campaign revealed in 2023, in which attackers seized privately owned routers to stage subsequent attacks on US critical infrastructure. Chairman Brendan Carr framed the action as the FCC continuing to do its part to secure America's critical supply chains. The commercial target is legible from the market data: Counterpoint Research puts Unitree at just under a fifth of global humanoid market share, and Sungrow Power Supply and the already heavily sanctioned Huawei lead inverters; Representative John Moolenaar welcomed the move, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has warned that Chinese AI firms could face sanctions over intellectual-property theft, and Unitree, Sungrow and Huawei did not immediately respond. The domestic side of the same trade got a number on the same day: Humanoid Global, a minority shareholder with no control over the transaction, disclosed that Agility Robotics has a definitive business combination agreement with Churchill Capital Corp XI at a 2.5 billion dollar pre-money equity value, expected to close in 2026 and to deliver more than 620 million dollars of gross proceeds, alongside a new 60,000-square-foot physical-AI development facility in Fremont, California adding roughly 200 technical and field-operations roles and more than 300 million dollars of multi-year Digit v5 orders subject to contractual milestones, with more than 65,000 operating hours accumulated across commitments at nine customer facilities.
